description_full: Dorman Products, Inc. supplies replacement and upgrade parts for the motor vehicle aftermarket industry in the United States and internationally. It operates through segments Light Duty, Heavy Duty, and Specialty Vehicle segments. The company offers engine products, including intake and exhaust manifolds, oil filters and coolers, fans, thermostat housings, and throttle bodies; undercar products, such as fluid lines, fluid reservoirs, connectors, 4-wheel drive components and axles, drain plugs, other engine, transmission, and axle components; steering and suspension products comprising control arms, ball joints, tie-rod ends, brake hardware and hydraulics, wheel and axle hardware, suspension arms, knuckles, links, bushings, and leaf springs, as well as other suspension, steering, and brake components; body products, including door handles and hinges, window lift motors, window regulators, switches and handles, wiper components, lighting, electrical, and other interior and exterior vehicle body components, including windshields for UTVs; electronics products, such as new and remanufactured modules, clusters and sensors; and hardware products consisting of threaded bolts and auto body fasteners, automotive and home electrical wiring components, and other hardware assortments and merchandise. It also provides OE FIX solutions, including exhaust manifolds, metal heater hose connectors, and aluminum oil filter housings; and intake manifolds, exhaust manifolds, oil filters and coolers, exhaust gas recirculation coolers, driveshafts, UTV windshields, and complex electronics modules. The company markets its products under the DORMAN, DORMAN OE FIX, HELP!, Conduct-Tite, Dayton Parts, SuperATV, Keller Performance Products, Assault Industries, Gboost, and GDP brands through aftermarket retailers, dealers, and national, regional, and local wholesale distributors and specialty markets. Dorman Products, Inc. was founded in 1918 and is headquartered in Colmar, Pennsylvania.

financial_summary: Dorman Products, Inc. is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $3.9B market cap on $2.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 12% against a 8% cost of capital, a 4-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 38%.

The business throws off $76M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders. Cash conversion is thin at 0.56×, however, which raises the oldest question in analysis: are these earnings backed by cash?.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.2× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 10.5×.

Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 13% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 14% operating margin runs 7pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+1.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted lower, down 8% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 15% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 0.75, it is more defensive than the market.
About $26.9M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 40% in the 2020 crash, 37% in the 2022 bear market and 54% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $65.37 (margin of safety -102%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 11%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $45.36 to $93.60 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/FCF 51.6 vs 16.7 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-4%).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 9 covering analysts target $159 on average, 20% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 12% earns above the cost of capital of 8.1%, but the 4pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.29).
It runs a 38% gross margin and converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: a Piotroski score of 8/9, but cash conversion of only 0.56x.
ROE of 14% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.7x equity multiplier).
It spends 2.1% of revenue on R&D and 0.9% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.2x net debt to EBITDA ($49.4M of cash against $439.9M of debt), with interest covered 10.5x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.8, in the safe zone).
Its debt comes due soon (maturity wall about 1.9 years out), so refinancing terms matter.
Working capital ties up about 311 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.1% over 3 years, 14.3% over 5 years and 10.2% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 12.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -11.1% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.7x depreciation (1.8% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 17.6% on average.
own: Insiders own 12.9%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 100%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $709K sold).
The share count has shrunk 1.3% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 3,871 employees, each generates about $550K of revenue, 1.4x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 10.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $20K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.5M (5x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
